Per-token pricing and reserved capacity tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04 14:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rajat Singh (Ventus), Evelyn Park (Ventus), Sanjay Patel (Ventus)

Summary: quick intro, then deep into unit economics: tokens per request, avg completion length, concurrency, budget. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private and levers (batching, KV cache, quant). Agreed to run benchmark and share pricing.

[00:00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam our SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Rajat: doing good thanks, thanks for arranging. we wanted to get into the cost side — we've been getting bills from other vendors and need to understand per unit economics, specifically for low-latency signals.
[00:00:18] Liam: cool, can you walk me through your workloads? like typical prompt length, completion length, and QPS?
[00:00:25] Rajat: yeah so our core algo is a trading signal gen, prompts are small, like 30-60 tokens, completions average 220 tokens but worst case up to 800 when we ask for expanded rationale. Peak QPS is around 75 but sustained is more like 20-30.
[00:00:42] Evelyn: and latency SLO is tight — p95 under 450ms for the short responses. tail is important because our execution pipeline depends on it.
[00:00:49] Maya: got it. so two axes: cost per token and latency SLO. we recommend different setups based on tradeoffs — hosted for speed to value, dedicated for predictable unit cost at volume, private for compliance.
[00:01:05] Sanjay: curious numbers — what's typical per-token for hosted vs dedicated? we saw a crazy range from other vendors.
[00:01:12] Liam: high level, for our curated open models we price per 1k tokens; rough ballpark numbers spoken off the cuff today: hosted might be around $0.80–$1.20 per 1k tokens for the larger variants, smaller model variants are cheaper, dedicated reserved capacity can reduce unit cost by ~30–50% depending on commit, and private has a larger fixed fee plus lower per-token op-ex. I'll follow up with a detailed sheet.
[00:01:36] Rajat: ok that range is useful, but we need an example calc. if we do 10M tokens a month with avg 250 tokens per call, what would we be looking at?
[00:01:45] Maya: quick math — 10M tokens is 10,000 * 1k tokens. at $1.00/1k that's $10k/month. if dedicated reduces by 40% that's about $6k/month, plus reserved commitment. But real savings often come from batching and caching.
[00:02:02] Evelyn: can you explain batching impact — we worry about batching because of latency.
[00:02:08] Liam: sure — continuous batching groups concurrent requests to increase GPU throughput. for small prompts it can increase GPU utilization significantly and reduce cost per-token, but it adds queuing latency in the tail. we tune target batch window and max latency; for your p95 450ms SLO, we've seen batching knobs that reduce costs ~15–30% without breaking p95 if tuned.
[00:02:28] Sanjay: what about caching — we have repeated instrument prompts across tickers, how would that behave?
[00:02:33] Liam: two forms: prefix/prompt caching and KV cache for decoder states. prefix caching returns cached completions for identical prompts (very cheap), and KV cache helps when you reuse the same context for many consecutive tokens in streaming scenarios — that reduces repeated compute for long histories. For repeated instrument-level prompts, prefix caching can cut cost on duplicate requests by ~50–90% depending on hit rate.
[00:02:53] Rajat: what's realistic cache hit for our domain? we have repeated templates with different tickers — maybe 30–40% canonical repeats?
[00:02:59] Maya: at 30% prefix hits you could see meaningful savings; combined with batching it's multiplicative on utilization. we'll run the benchmark to estimate realistic hit rates.
[00:03:09] [00:03:10] Speaker 1: sorry question about model variants — are smaller models (7B) fast enough for your use-case?
[00:03:15] Liam: yes for many signal tasks 7B with 4-bit quant often hits similar accuracy to 13B on templated prompts, but quality tests required. 7B gives lower latency and better batching efficiency. for edge-case explanations you may want a mid-sized 13B/34B. part of our POC is to test different model sizes and quantization.
[00:03:35] Evelyn: what about quantization risks? debugability, hallucination changes?
[00:03:40] Liam: quantization can slightly affect calibration; we recommend eval sets and regression alerts. Redwood's optimize tooling suggests quant profiles per workload and flags quality regressions tied to prompt sets.
[00:03:52] Rajat: ok, security and data retention — if we go hosted, can you guarantee no persisted customer data beyond tokens used? we have regulatory constraints.
[00:03:59] Maya: hosted offers configurable data retention policies, by default ephemeral for queries, and enterprise plans can enable customer-managed KMS, SOC 2 logs, and contract language around retention. private gives you full control. we'll attach the security pack with specifics.
[00:04:14] Sanjay: for Dedicated — what commit sizes make sense to hit that 30–50% saving?
[00:04:20] Liam: it's a function of GPU type and your concurrency pattern. typical sweet spot on our Dedicated product is 2–8 reserved GPUs for sustained throughput; at high sustained volumes, reserved contracts and autoscaling burst reduce marginal cost. I'll model it with your 10M tokens to show break-even.
[00:04:35] Rajat: timeline — we'd like a pilot within 2–3 weeks to run against our latency-sensitive pipeline.
[00:04:40] Maya: that's doable — we'll kick off bench, provision a dedicated trial if you want to see reserved capacity math, or run on hosted first to get quick numbers.
[00:04:48] Evelyn: we need the team who'd own the infra deep-dive — Liam and our infra lead (Evelyn) should sync on networking (VPC peering, egress rules) and key management.
[00:04:59] Liam: yep we'll cover VPC, SAML SSO, and HSM/KMS setup. for private we also discuss air-gapped deploys and offline model validation but that's further down the line.
[00:05:10] [00:05:12] Maya: quick note on cost modeling levers: 1) pick model variant 2) enable quantization 3) use prefix caching 4) tune batching windows 5) move to reserved/dedicated pools. each has latency/quality tradeoffs.
[00:05:25] Sanjay: can you show an example of the math including batching?
[00:05:29] Liam: example — baseline: 250 tokens/order at $1.00/1k = $0.25 per request; with 30% prefix cache hit effective tokens billed drop to 175 average which is $0.175 per request; batching improvements might reduce per-token execution inefficiencies so effective cost could drop another 15% to ~$0.15/request. multiply by volume gives your monthly.
[00:05:48] Rajat: that seems promising. what about tail latency with batching and dedicated GPUs?
[00:05:53] Liam: dedicated pools let you control queueing and priority; you can reserve capacity for low-latency lanes and enable burst for cost efficiency. we can set SLO-based routing so critical requests hit low-latency nodes while others get best-effort batching.
[00:06:09] [00:06:10] Speaker 2: small transcription hiccup — "KV catch" should be KV cache.
[00:06:14] Maya: haha yes KV cache — ty.
[00:06:18] Evelyn: what's required from our side to run the benchmark?
[00:06:21] Maya: we need a representative prompt set, expected QPS profile, and any latency SLOs. we'll provide a test harness and a script to replay traffic.
[00:06:29] Sanjay: about private — we may need on-prem for some desks, is that single-tenant or hybrid?
[00:06:34] Liam: Private can be VPC-hosted or on-prem. hybrid patterns are common: control plane in your VPC, compute in your network or partner colo. pricing includes a setup fee plus lower per-token operational rate. it's normally considered when you have strict compliance or cost at scale that warrants the fixed setup.
[00:06:52] Rajat: can you include the egress/ingress network cost assumptions in the pricing? we have big data movement concerns.
[00:06:58] Maya: yes we'll include network egress assumptions and separate them out so you can model it.
[00:07:03] [00:07:10] Liam: also want to call out model compilation — we select optimized kernels and sequence-length-aware kernels which matter for small prompts and reduce compute; that also impacts unit cost.
[00:07:21] Rajat: curious if you support function/tool-calls and streaming for our pipeline — streaming helps reduce p95 in some cases.
[00:07:27] Liam: we do streaming and function calling; streaming reduces end-to-end latency for long responses since you can start processing before completion. KV cache + streaming is a good combo.
[00:07:37] Evelyn: ok let's talk numbers we want in the sheet: per-1k token rates for 7B/13B/34B both hosted and dedicated, expected percent savings at 10M/50M/200M tokens, quantization effect, and typical batching/caching assumptions.
[00:07:50] Maya: noted. we'll build a scenario table and include break-even for reserved commits.
[00:07:55] Sanjay: any gotchas about billing granularity? we bill per token but do you prorate for partial tokens?
[00:08:01] Liam: billing is per 1k token granularity in the sheet but actual metering is token-level; we'll show both ways.
[00:08:08] Rajat: good. will you share reliability SLAs for Dedicated?
[00:08:12] Maya: yes Dedicated comes with SLA targets and uptime credits; we'll include the SLA doc in the pack.
[00:08:18] [00:08:20] Speaker 3: minor audio — "reduced by 40 percent" sounded like dedicated only; clarify that it's range.
[00:08:24] Maya: yes it's a range depending on model, GPUs, and commit. we'll provide modeled examples.
[00:08:30] Evelyn: any references from other quant funds you've worked with? case studies?
[00:08:34] Maya: we can redact names but we have a couple of hedge funds that ran similar pilots; we'll include anonymized results and cost regressed examples.
[00:08:43] Sanjay: timeline again — we want numbers in a week and bench started within 10 business days.
[00:08:49] Maya: we'll aim to deliver pricing and security pack by EOD 2026-03-05 and have Liam kick off bench by 2026-03-06.
[00:08:58] [00:09:05] long silence while someone checks doc, small cross talk
[00:09:22] Liam: quick technical note — for low-latency lanes we can pin smaller models to specific GPUs and use KV caching to avoid recomputation; that reduces jitter.
[00:09:33] Rajat: sweet. anything else on cost levers?
[00:09:36] Liam: also think about caching at app level, not just infra — if you can approximate cheaper checks in the app and only call the model for edge cases you'll reduce billed tokens.
[00:09:46] Maya: agreed.
[00:09:48] Evelyn: ok we'll loop in legal to start reviewing the security pack once you send it.
[00:09:53] Maya: perfect. I'll send calendar invite for the next technical sync.
[00:09:58] [00:10:05] brief wrap-up: recap of next steps and owners (see action items).

Notes (transcription has small errors; some speaker labels generic). End of call.
